coverageDimensions:
SERVICE coverage — this is the only dimension the page supplies, and it supplies it cleanly. It means: of the AWS services that exist, which ones can consume a Secrets Manager secret. The page names 56 as a numerator. It does NOT give a denominator: the total count of AWS services is nowhere on the page, so any percentage needs an external service list, and the mismatch noted above (tools and features listed alongside services) makes that reconciliation lossy. Report the 56 as a named set; do not report a percentage sourced from this page.

REGION coverage — the page gives nothing. It would mean: in which AWS Regions does each integration work. Not a single Region name, Region code, partition, or "available in all Regions where the service is offered" sentence appears. There is no per-Region column and no availability note. Any Region figure attached to this capability from this page would be fabricated.

RESOURCE TYPE coverage — the page gives nothing. It would mean: which resource types Secrets Manager can hold or attach credentials for (secretsmanager:Secret, rds:DBInstance, ecs:TaskDefinition and so on). No resource type name, ARN pattern, or CloudFormation type appears. The one Secrets Manager resource, the secret, is implicit in the title and never enumerated. Resource types may exist on the 56 child pages; on this page there are none.

Second dimension: none. There is no matrix — no scan method, no capability column, no per-Region split — so each of the 56 values carries exactly one status and no qualifier.

features.featureName: AWS services that use AWS Secrets Manager secrets
features.reasoning:
The axis values are the names of OTHER AWS services — App Runner, Amazon Aurora, AWS Transfer Family — not anything Secrets Manager publishes about itself, so the axis is `service` and the kind is external: the set of AWS services exists whether or not Secrets Manager does. That makes a ratio meaningful in principle (56 out of all AWS services), though the denominator is not on this page. Counted by hand off the Topics list: 56 entries, no duplicates.

The list is one capability, not several: every entry is a member of the same relation ("this service consumes a Secrets Manager secret"). The child pages differentiate HOW — managed rotation, direct retrieval, credential injection — but this page states none of that, so splitting into sub-capabilities here would be inventing distinctions the page does not make.

Two cautions on the values themselves. Several entries are not cloud services with resources: AWS SCT, AWS Toolkit for JetBrains and AWS App2Container are client-side tools; AWS Marketplace and AWS Managed Services are programs. Several others are features, not services: Amazon Redshift query editor v2 sits under Amazon Redshift (both listed), and AWS Glue DataBrew and AWS Glue Studio are both Glue-family. Reconciling these 56 labels against a canonical AWS service list will not be one-to-one, and the page offers no service codes or ARN namespaces to reconcile with. Take the link TEXT as the value; the link targets carry internal codes (_ARlong, _APSYlong, _EMXlong, _QS for Amazon Quick) and one outright typo (integrationg_how-services-use-secrets_TIME.md), so filenames are not identifiers.
features.statuses: 56 stated as supported, 0 stated as not supported. There is no Yes/No column, no footnote, no "not supported" prose, and nothing marked retired or deprecated. Support is asserted by the H1 acting as a predicate over the list: every entry under "AWS services that use AWS Secrets Manager secrets" is, by the page's own framing, a service that uses them. The critical consequence: this is a positive-only closed list. A service absent from the 56 (Lambda, S3, CloudFormation, Step Functions and so on) is NOT documented here as unsupported — the page is silent about it. A coverage map must record 56 positives and zero negatives, and must never synthesise a negative from omission on this page.

pageTitle: AWS services that use AWS Secrets Manager secrets
shouldNotExtract:
The entire "See also" section, and in particular the boilerplate bullet about optional AI coding assistant skills — the `aws agent-toolkit search-skills --search-query secretsmanager` command and the Agent Toolkit for AWS link. That is appended to every AWS page now and is not coverage of anything.

Also not coverage: the `<a name="integrating">` anchor; the `.md` link targets and their internal code suffixes; the word "Topics" itself as a heading. And nothing on this page should produce a Region value, a resource type, a quota, a price, or an API operation, because the page contains none.
trap:
The trap is the rule "never take a Topics block". Applied mechanically here it extracts zero, which is wrong — the H1 states what the list means, and the page has no other body. The correct condition is narrow: harvest a Topics block only when the H1 itself predicates the list ("AWS services that use...", "Supported resource types for...") and there is no competing body content. A parser that instead harvests Topics blocks unconditionally will manufacture false coverage on every ordinary AWS parent page, which is the worse failure of the two.

The second trap is manufacturing negatives. This page is a positive-only list, so a parser that computes "56 of ~200 AWS services covered, therefore Lambda is not supported" is inventing a claim AWS did not make. Absence here means silence, not exclusion.

Third: assuming the list is alphabetical and normalising or de-duplicating on that assumption. It is not sorted — Amazon Q, Amazon OpenSearch Ingestion, AWS OpsWorks for Chef Automate and Amazon Quick run out of order. Fourth: deriving values from link filenames rather than link text, which yields "TIME" from a misspelled file, "QS" for Amazon Quick, and "ARlong"/"APSYlong" for App Runner and AppSync. Fifth: reading "Amazon Redshift query editor v2", "AWS Glue Studio" and "AWS Glue DataBrew" as top-level services, or reading "Direct Connect" (listed without the AWS prefix) as a different thing from AWS Direct Connect.
whatThePageStates:
This is a parent/index page whose entire body is a Topics list. It has no prose, no table, no footnotes — the H1 is the claim and the list is the evidence: these are the AWS services that use AWS Secrets Manager secrets, each linking to a child page describing how that service uses them. The only other content is a "See also" bullet about optional AI-coding-assistant skills.

This makes the page an unusual case: on almost every AWS page the Topics block is navigation and must be discarded, but here the H1 itself gives the list its meaning, so the Topics block IS the enumeration. It states one axis only — service names — and states them positively only. There is no Region, no resource type, no Yes/No column, no exclusion, and no second dimension anywhere on the page.
